entries.description: List available issue statuses in a Linear team

entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Linear__save_issue
entries.description: Create or update a Linear issue. If `id` is provided, updates the existing issue; otherwise creates a new one. When creating, `team` is required, and `title` is required unless `template` is set. Note: use `assignee` (not `assigneeId`) to set the assignee — it accepts a user ID, name, email, or "me".

id.description: Only for updating an existing issue. Pass the issue ID or identifier (e.g., LIN-123). Do NOT pass this parameter when creating a new issue.

title.description: Issue title (required when creating, unless template is set)

description.description: Content as Markdown. Do not escape the string — use literal newlines and special characters, not escape sequences. To mention a user, use @displayName (e.g., @johndoe)

patch.description: Partial edits applied to the current content, in order and atomically (one failing operation aborts the whole save). Every anchor string must match the current content exactly once. Only valid on update, in place of the full content/description field

old_string.description: Exact text to replace. Must match the current content exactly once

new_string.description: Replacement text. Empty string deletes the match

replace_all.description: Replace every occurrence instead of requiring a unique match

anchor.description: Exact text to insert before. Must match the current content exactly once

text.description: Text to insert directly before the anchor. Include separators (e.g. "\n\n")

anchor.description: Exact text to insert after. Must match the current content exactly once

text.description: Text to insert directly after the anchor. Include separators (e.g. "\n\n")
Text to insert at the very start of the content
Text to insert at the very end of the content

from.description: Exact text where the range starts (inclusive). Must match exactly once

to.description: Exact text where the range ends (exclusive, stays in place). Must match exactly once after `from`

new_string.description: Text replacing the range. Empty string deletes it

team.description: Team name or ID (required when creating)

template.description: Template name or ID. Applied on create only. The template fills in the content, fields, and sub-issues server-side. A `description` replaces the template body rather than merging with it, but an empty `description` keeps the template body. Labels merge with the template's own

cycle.description: Cycle name, number, or ID. Null to remove

project.description: Project name, ID, identifier (e.g., P-ENG-123), or slug. Null to remove

assignee.description: User ID, name, email, or "me". Null to remove

delegate.description: Agent name or ID. When the user asks to delegate to "Linear" or "the Linear agent", this refers to the "Linear" app user specifically. Null to remove

labels.description: Label names or IDs as a JSON array of strings (e.g. ["Bug", "Urgent"]). Replaces the full label set; existing labels not included are removed. Omit to leave labels unchanged. Cannot be combined with addLabels/removeLabels; prefer those for incremental changes

addLabels.description: Label names or IDs as a JSON array of strings (e.g. ["Bug", "Urgent"]) to add. Append-only; existing labels are never removed. Cannot be combined with a team change

removeLabels.description: Label names or IDs as a JSON array of strings (e.g. ["Bug", "Urgent"]) to remove. Only valid when updating an existing issue. Cannot be combined with a team change

dueDate.description: Due date (ISO format). On update, pass null to remove the due date

slaBreachesAt.description: ISO-8601 timestamp when the SLA will breach. On update, pass null to remove the SLA

slaType.description: SLA day counting type: "all" or "onlyBusinessDays". Only use with slaBreachesAt; null means unset

parentId.description: Parent issue ID or identifier (e.g., LIN-123). Null to remove

estimate.description: Issue estimate value. On create, pass null or omit for no estimate. On update, pass null to clear the estimate; omitting leaves it unchanged. 0 is a real estimate only on teams that allow zero estimates.

links.description: Link attachments to add [{url, title}]. Append-only; existing links are never removed

setReleases.description: Replace all releases on the issue with these. Cannot be combined with addReleases/removeReleases

addReleases.description: Release IDs or slugs to add. Append-only; existing releases are never removed

removeReleases.description: Release IDs or slugs to remove. Only valid when updating an existing issue

blocks.description: Issue IDs/identifiers this blocks. Append-only; existing relations are never removed

blockedBy.description: Issue IDs/identifiers blocking this. Append-only; existing relations are never removed

relatedTo.description: Related issue IDs/identifiers. Append-only; existing relations are never removed

duplicateOf.description: Duplicate of issue ID/identifier. Null to remove

removeBlockedBy.description: Issue IDs/identifiers to remove as blockers of this issue

{"id":"SMA-822","uuid":"39a23478-c510-4fbf-ba10-81a764a02ebc","title":"Move the sqlx sqlite feature out of the workspace base so Postgres-only users do not compile C SQLite","description":"## Problem

The workspace `sqlx` pin in the root `Cargo.toml` enables the `sqlite` feature. All crates that use `sqlx` inherit it. Thus every user of `paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres` compiles `libsqlite3-sys` with bundled C SQLite, although the Postgres backend uses no SQLite code.

This matters for advisories. RUSTSEC-2026-0459 (<issue id="ca826652-1713-4b1a-851e-f0abb9fe2308" label="SMA-763" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-763/ignore-rustsec-2026-0459-libsqlite3-sys-037-until-sqlx-allows" />) flagged the bundled SQLite, and it also affected Postgres-only users.

## Proposal

* Remove `sqlite` from the workspace `sqlx` feature list.
* Add `features = ["sqlite"]` in `paigasus-helikon-sessions-sqlite` and `paigasus-helikon-evals` (the `trace-sqlite` feature).
* Make sure that `sessions-postgres` still builds. It uses `sqlx::migrate!`, so check that the `migrate` and `macros` features work without `sqlite`.

## Done when

* `cargo tree -p paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres -i libsqlite3-sys` shows no path.
* All CI gates pass, including `sessions-it` and `build-no-default-features`.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/smaschek/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/7.0.2/skills/brainstorming

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
propose something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

brainstorming:

  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.

  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice

  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece

# release-plz.toml — automated versioning, changelogs, GitHub releases.
# Reference: https://release-plz.dev/docs/config

[workspace]
# Makes the release PR run `cargo update` on `Cargo.lock`. It does not cascade
# version bumps. release-plz gives a dependent crate that has no commits of its
# own a patch bump only (release-plz#1599). For a breaking bump, see
# docs/runbooks/release-ascend.md, section "A breaking change in a crate with
# dependents" (SMA-838).
dependencies_update = true

# Force the scopeless release-PR title + commit (`chore: release`). release-plz's
# default SINGLE-crate template is `chore({package}): release {version}`, which uses
# the full package name (e.g. `paigasus-helikon`) as the Conventional-Commits scope —
# not in the convco/.versionrc + pr-title.yml allowlist (which uses short scopes like
# `facade`), so both the `commits` and `pr-title` gates reject it. The scopeless form
# matches the historical multi-crate release PRs and REDACTEDes both. (Diagnosed on PR #58,
# the first facade-only release.)
pr_name = "chore: release"

# All library crates publish to crates.io (Stage 1 SMA-385 onward; the last
# stubs ascended in SMA-332/SMA-333). Remaining per-package overrides below
# are the only exceptions. See CLAUDE.md for the 4-step recipe a stub
# follows when it ascends.

[changelog]
sort_commits = "newest"

# Internal test members (three harnesses and one helper library): these four workspace members never publish.
# publish = false in each Cargo.toml and release = false here MUST move
# together.

# Internal cross-runtime HTTP wire-format conformance suite: boots BOTH the axum
# and actix runtimes and asserts byte/structural parity. Never published, so it
# carries the publish=false / release=false pair.
[[package]]
name = "paigasus-helikon-runtime-http-conformance"
publish = false
release = false

Here is your request in my words. Today the root `sqlx` pin turns on `sqlite` for every crate that uses `sqlx`. You want `sqlite` turned on only where it is used: `sessions-sqlite` and `evals` (`trace-sqlite`). Then a Postgres-only user does not compile bundled C SQLite. That user also does not get SQLite advisories like RUSTSEC-2026-0459.

What I found:

- **Three crates use the workspace `sqlx`:** `sessions-postgres`, `sessions-sqlite`, and `evals`. No other crate uses it.
- **There are two SQLite paths into `sessions-postgres` today.** One goes through `sqlx-sqlite`. The other goes through `sqlx-macros-core`, the proc-macro behind `migrate!`. If you remove the feature, both paths go away.
- **`PgPool` is in the public API of `sessions-postgres`.** A downstream user who got `sqlx::sqlite` only through our crate loses it. I think a patch release is correct, because we never promised that feature. I will write this in the spec.
- **Release risk.** release-plz decides which crates to bump from the files that change in each crate. The fix is in the root `Cargo.toml`, so `sessions-postgres` may get no release. Then crates.io keeps the old manifest, which includes SQLite. To prevent this, I will update the comment at `crates/paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres/Cargo.toml:18`, which says "on top of the workspace sqlx base". I will also use a `fix(sessions)` PR title.

One decision is open: **do we add a CI guard so that SQLite cannot come back?**

1. **A guard step in `build-no-default-features` (my pick).** The step fails if `cargo tree -p paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres -i libsqlite3-sys` finds a path. It uses the same pattern as the axum and protox checks in that job. It only resolves the dependency graph, so it adds about one second. Without a guard, a later edit to the root pin can bring SQLite back and no gate fails.
2. **No guard.** The change is smaller, but nothing stops a regression.

Which do you want? Tell me if any part of my summary is wrong.

# SMA-822: Move the sqlx `sqlite` feature out of the workspace base

Linear: [SMA-822](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-822). Size: a small change.

## Intent

The root `[workspace.dependencies]` pin of `sqlx` enables the `sqlite` feature.
Every crate that uses `sqlx` inherits it. Thus every user of
`paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres` compiles `libsqlite3-sys` with bundled C
SQLite, and gets every SQLite advisory (for example RUSTSEC-2026-0459, SMA-763),
although the Postgres backend uses no SQLite code.

The baseline on `main` (52a74cca) has two paths from `sessions-postgres` to
`libsqlite3-sys`:

```text
libsqlite3-sys v0.40.0 └── sqlx-sqlite └── sqlx └── paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres
libsqlite3-sys v0.40.0 └── sqlx-sqlite └── sqlx-macros-core └── sqlx-macros (proc-macro) └── sqlx
```

## Goals

- Only the crates that use SQLite enable the `sqlx` `sqlite` feature:
  `paigasus-helikon-sessions-sqlite` and `paigasus-helikon-evals` (through its
  `trace-sqlite` feature).
- `cargo tree -p paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres -i libsqlite3-sys -e normal,build`
  finds no path.
- A CI step fails if SQLite comes back into the `sessions-postgres` graph.
- The published `sessions-postgres` manifest on crates.io loses `sqlite` in the
  next release.

## Non-goals

- No change to the Rust code of any crate.
- No change to the `deny.toml` or `.cargo/audit.toml` advisory lists.
- No change to how `sessions-sqlite` builds SQLite (bundled stays).

## Anti-goals

- `sessions-postgres` must not lose `migrate!` or the `macros` feature.
- `sessions-sqlite` and `evals --features trace-sqlite` must not lose any `sqlx`
  feature that they have today.

## Constraints

- Workspace inheritance is mandatory (CLAUDE.md). Each crate keeps
  `sqlx = { workspace = true, ... }` and adds its own `features`.
- `sqlx` types are in the public API: `PgPool` in `sessions-postgres`,
  `SqlitePool` in `sessions-sqlite`. A downstream crate that used
  `sqlx::sqlite` only because `sessions-postgres` turned it on stops compiling.
  We never documented that feature as part of the `sessions-postgres` API, so
  this change is a patch release, not a breaking release. The CHANGELOG entry
  from the `fix` commit says that the feature is gone.
- release-plz bumps a crate from the commits that touch files in that crate's
  directory. A change to the root `Cargo.toml` only does not get a release for
  `sessions-postgres`, so crates.io keeps the old manifest. Each of the three
  crates must have a file change in its own directory. Each `Cargo.toml` changes
  anyway (`sessions-sqlite` and `evals` get `features = ["sqlite"]`,
  `sessions-postgres` gets the corrected comment). The PR title uses the `fix`
  type, so the squashed commit gives a patch bump. The facade cascade is
  automatic; no version is bumped by hand.

## Approaches

1. **Remove only `sqlite` from the base (chosen).** The base keeps
   `runtime-tokio`, `macros`, and `migrate`, which all three crates use. Each
   SQLite crate adds `features = ["sqlite"]`. This is the smallest change and
   matches the ticket.
2. **Make the base minimal (`runtime-tokio` only).** Each crate lists every
   feature it uses. This is more explicit, but it changes three crates' feature
   lists for no user gain. All three crates use `macros` and `migrate` today.
3. **Add a second workspace entry (`sqlx-sqlite`).** Cargo does not allow two
   `[workspace.dependencies]` keys for one package without a rename. A rename
   changes the name in the code. Rejected.

## Design

1. Root `Cargo.toml`, line 84: remove `"sqlite"` from the `sqlx` feature list.
   Result: `features = ["runtime-tokio", "macros", "migrate"]`.
2. `crates/paigasus-helikon-sessions-sqlite/Cargo.toml`:
   `sqlx = { workspace = true, features = ["sqlite"] }`.
3. `crates/paigasus-helikon-evals/Cargo.toml`:
   `sqlx = { workspace = true, optional = true, features = ["sqlite"] }`.
   `trace-sqlite = ["dep:sqlx"]` stays.
4. `crates/paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres/Cargo.toml`: update the comment on
   line 18 so that it names the new base (`runtime-tokio`, `macros`, `migrate`,
   and no `sqlite`).
5. `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, job `build-no-default-features`: add a step
   `Assert no SQLite under sessions-postgres`. It runs
   `cargo tree -p paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres -e normal,build -i libsqlite3-sys`
   and fails if the output names `libsqlite3-sys`. It must test the output, not
   the exit code. The builder must confirm what `cargo tree -i` prints and
   returns when the package is not in the graph, before and after the change.
   The step uses the same shape as the existing axum and `vendored-protox`
   steps: an `::error::` line that says what to fix. It resolves the graph only,
   so it does not build.
6. The step also checks the facade with only `sessions-postgres` on:
   `cargo tree -p paigasus-helikon --no-default-features --features sessions-postgres -e normal,build -i libsqlite3-sys`.
   This is the path most users take.
7. Update `docs/runbooks/ci-architecture.md` with one line about the new step
   in the `build-no-default-features` section, if that section lists its steps.

## Book and README

The mdBook and the crate READMEs do not name the `sqlx` features, so they need
no change. The builder confirms this with a search for `sqlite` in
`docs/book/src` and in the three crates' `README.md`.

## Verification

- The `cargo tree` command from the ticket finds no path.
- The guard fails on `main` (mutation check: put `"sqlite"` back into the base
  and run the step locally) and passes on the branch.
- `cargo build -p paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres` (lib only, no dev-deps)
  passes, so `migrate!` works without `sqlite`.
- `cargo build -p paigasus-helikon-sessions-sqlite` and
  `cargo build -p paigasus-helikon-evals --features trace-sqlite` pass alone.
- `cargo build -p paigasus-helikon-evals --no-default-features` passes.
- All CI gates from CLAUDE.md pass locally where possible. `sessions-it` runs
  in CI.

## Left to the builder

- The exact text of the `Cargo.toml` comment and the `::error::` message.
- Whether the runbook needs the line (item 7).

# SMA-822: Move the sqlx `sqlite` feature out of the workspace base

Linear: [SMA-822](https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-822). Size: a small change.

## Intent

The root `[workspace.dependencies]` pin of `sqlx` enables the `sqlite` feature.
Every crate that uses `sqlx` inherits it. Thus every user of
`paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres` compiles `libsqlite3-sys` with bundled C
SQLite, and gets every SQLite advisory (for example RUSTSEC-2026-0459, SMA-763),
although the Postgres backend uses no SQLite code.

The baseline on `main` (52a74cca) has two paths from `sessions-postgres` to
`libsqlite3-sys`:

```text
libsqlite3-sys v0.40.0 └── sqlx-sqlite └── sqlx └── paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres
libsqlite3-sys v0.40.0 └── sqlx-sqlite └── sqlx-macros-core └── sqlx-macros (proc-macro) └── sqlx
```

## Goals

- Only the crates that use SQLite enable the `sqlx` `sqlite` feature:
  `paigasus-helikon-sessions-sqlite` and `paigasus-helikon-evals` (through its
  `trace-sqlite` feature).
- `cargo tree -p paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres -i libsqlite3-sys -e normal,build`
  finds no path.
- A CI step fails if SQLite comes back into the `sessions-postgres` graph.
- The published `sessions-postgres` manifest on crates.io loses `sqlite` in the
  next release.

## Non-goals

- No change to the Rust code of any crate.
- No change to the `deny.toml` or `.cargo/audit.toml` advisory lists.
- No change to how `sessions-sqlite` builds SQLite (bundled stays).

## Anti-goals

- `sessions-postgres` must not lose `migrate!` or the `macros` feature.
- `sessions-sqlite` and `evals --features trace-sqlite` must not lose any `sqlx`
  feature that they have today.

## Constraints

- Workspace inheritance is mandatory (CLAUDE.md). Each crate keeps
  `sqlx = { workspace = true, ... }` and adds its own `features`.
- `sqlx` types are in the public API: `PgPool` in `sessions-postgres`,
  `SqlitePool` in `sessions-sqlite`. A downstream crate that used
  `sqlx::sqlite` only because `sessions-postgres` turned it on stops compiling.
  We never documented that feature as part of the `sessions-postgres` API, so
  this change is a patch release, not a breaking release. The CHANGELOG entry
  from the `fix` commit says that the feature is gone.
- release-plz bumps a crate from the commits that touch files in that crate's
  directory. A change to the root `Cargo.toml` only does not get a release for
  `sessions-postgres`, so crates.io keeps the old manifest. Each of the three
  crates must have a file change in its own directory. Each `Cargo.toml` changes
  anyway (`sessions-sqlite` and `evals` get `features = ["sqlite"]`,
  `sessions-postgres` gets the corrected comment). The PR title uses the `fix`
  type, so the squashed commit gives a patch bump. The facade cascade is
  automatic; no version is bumped by hand.

## Approaches

1. **Remove only `sqlite` from the base (chosen).** The base keeps
   `runtime-tokio`, `macros`, and `migrate`, which all three crates use. Each
   SQLite crate adds `features = ["sqlite"]`. This is the smallest change and
   matches the ticket.
2. **Make the base minimal (`runtime-tokio` only).** Each crate lists every
   feature it uses. This is more explicit, but it changes three crates' feature
   lists for no user gain. All three crates use `macros` and `migrate` today.
3. **Add a second workspace entry (`sqlx-sqlite`).** Cargo does not allow two
   `[workspace.dependencies]` keys for one package without a rename. A rename
   changes the name in the code. Rejected.

## Design

1. Root `Cargo.toml`, line 84: remove `"sqlite"` from the `sqlx` feature list.
   Result: `features = ["runtime-tokio", "macros", "migrate"]`.
2. `crates/paigasus-helikon-sessions-sqlite/Cargo.toml`:
   `sqlx = { workspace = true, features = ["sqlite"] }`.
3. `crates/paigasus-helikon-evals/Cargo.toml`:
   `sqlx = { workspace = true, optional = true, features = ["sqlite"] }`.
   `trace-sqlite = ["dep:sqlx"]` stays.
4. `crates/paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres/Cargo.toml`: update the comment on
   line 18 so that it names the new base (`runtime-tokio`, `macros`, `migrate`,
   and no `sqlite`).
5. `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, job `build-no-default-features`: add a step
   `Assert no SQLite under sessions-postgres`. It runs
   `cargo tree -p paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres -e normal,build -i libsqlite3-sys`
   and fails if the output names `libsqlite3-sys`. It must test the output, not
   the exit code. The builder must confirm what `cargo tree -i` prints and
   returns when the package is not in the graph, before and after the change.
   The step uses the same shape as the existing axum and `vendored-protox`
   steps: an `::error::` line that says what to fix. It resolves the graph only,
   so it does not build.
6. The step also checks the facade with only `sessions-postgres` on:
   `cargo tree -p paigasus-helikon --no-default-features --features sessions-postgres -e normal,build -i libsqlite3-sys`.
   This is the path most users take.
7. Update `docs/runbooks/ci-architecture.md` with one line about the new step
   in the `build-no-default-features` section, if that section lists its steps.

## Book and README

The mdBook and the crate READMEs do not name the `sqlx` features, so they need
no change. The builder confirms this with a search for `sqlite` in
`docs/book/src` and in the three crates' `README.md`.

## Verification

- The `cargo tree` command from the ticket finds no path.
- The guard fails on `main` (mutation check: put `"sqlite"` back into the base
  and run the step locally) and passes on the branch.
- `cargo build -p paigasus-helikon-sessions-postgres` (lib only, no dev-deps)
  passes, so `migrate!` works without `sqlite`.
- `cargo build -p paigasus-helikon-sessions-sqlite` and
  `cargo build -p paigasus-helikon-evals --features trace-sqlite` pass alone.
- `cargo build -p paigasus-helikon-evals --no-default-features` passes.
- All CI gates from CLAUDE.md pass locally where possible. `sessions-it` runs

- Whether the runbook needs the line (item 7).

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## What this is

The Paigasus AI SDK (codename **Helikon**, after Mt Helicon where Pegasus's hoof struck the Hippocrene spring). A Rust SDK for building AI agents. All crates live under the `paigasus-helikon-*` namespace.

The full architectural reference lives in Notion: ["Crate Reference"](https://www.notion.so/355830e8fbaa813c92e8c1aa9985fd3f). Linear project: `Paigasus Helikon` (issues prefixed `SMA-`).

## Common commands

```bash
cargo build --workspace                              # all 14 crates
cargo build --workspace --all-features               # facade with every optional crate
cargo run -p paigasus-helikon-cli --bin helikon
cargo run -p paigasus-helikon-cli --bin paigasus-helikon
```

To reproduce **every** CI gate locally (matches `.github/workflows/ci.yml` job-for-job):

```bash
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace --all-features
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --all-features --no-deps
DOC_COVERAGE_THRESHOLD=80 NIGHTLY_CHANNEL=nightly-2026-05-01 \
  bash scripts/check-doc-coverage.sh                 # requires: rustup toolchain install nightly-2026-05-01
npm ci                                               # once, or after package-lock.json changes
npx markdownlint-cli2                                # reads .markdownlint-cli2.jsonc
bash scripts/check-markdownlint-config.sh            # asserts that config is in force
bash scripts/check-cargo-profile-env-sync.sh         # cargo-visible workflow env is uniform
bash scripts/check-cargo-profile-env-sync-selftest.sh # …and its parser still parses (fmt runs both)
bash scripts/check-release-gaps-selftest.sh            # release gap report + release-plz.yml guards (fmt runs it)
bash scripts/check-breaking-cascade-selftest.sh      # the cascade guard keeps its rule (fmt runs it)
bash scripts/check-breaking-cascade.sh                 # breaking bump needs breaking dependents (PR only; fmt runs it)
```

The full list lives in `CONTRIBUTING.md` (single source of truth for contributor policies).

## Workspace layout

15 crates under `crates/`. The facade `paigasus-helikon` re-exports `paigasus-helikon-core` unconditionally and the other 12 sibling crates behind Cargo features.

Every crate carries a real implementation and publishes to crates.io; zero name-claim stubs remain (first published in SMA-385, last ascends in SMA-333). One standing exception: `paigasus-helikon-cli` publishes as a **binary** crate — its lib target is internal (`missing_docs` opted out), carries no stability guarantee, and exists only so `cargo install paigasus-helikon-cli` resolves. `paigasus-helikon-sessions-testkit` publishes as a normal library crate (SMA-805); the three session backends keep a path-only dev-dependency on it. Exact versions move every release — read each crate's `Cargo.toml`, don't trust numbers written here.

Workspace inheritance is **mandatory**: per-crate `Cargo.toml`s only set `name`, `description`, and any crate-specific bits. Everything else (`edition`, `rust-version`, `authors`, `license`, `repository`, `homepage`, `keywords`, `categories`) inherits from `[workspace.package]` in the root `Cargo.toml`. Don't hardcode these per-crate.

**Per-crate version is the one exception.** No stubs remain, so the 4-step ascend recipe is now historical — but two caveats still bite any PR that hand-bumps a version:

- **If a crate uses `paigasus-helikon-core` API added in the *same* PR, bump `core` too**, along with its `[workspace.dependencies]` pin and CHANGELOG. `cargo publish --verify` builds the tarball against the **registry** core, so otherwise the publish fails and release-plz deadlocks.
- **Any PR that hand-bumps a sibling must ALSO bump the facade** (`crates/paigasus-helikon/Cargo.toml` version + its self-pin + CHANGELOG). release-plz does not bump the facade for a sibling version that is already at target when the PR merges, so a manual bump silently leaves the facade advertising stale dep reqs. (`dependencies_update = true` only makes the release PR run `cargo update` on `Cargo.lock`; it does not cascade version bumps.)
- **A breaking bump of a crate needs a breaking bump of each crate that depends on it.** release-plz gives a dependent without its own commits only a patch bump (release-plz#1599), and users then get two copies of the crate. The `fmt` job runs `scripts/check-breaking-cascade.sh` to enforce this. See `docs/runbooks/release-ascend.md` → "A breaking change in a crate with dependents".
- Feature branches must match the `branch-names` ruleset (`feature/**` or `hotfix/**`); a `chore/**` branch is rejected at push with `GH013 … creations being restricted`.

Full lifecycle, the 4-step recipe, and the SMA-321/SMA-346 postmortems: `docs/runbooks/release-ascend.md`.

Third-party version pins live in `[workspace.dependencies]` (root). Members reference them via `dep.workspace = true`. Internal crate paths are also in `[workspace.dependencies]` so the facade can use `workspace = true` consistently.

## Non-obvious patterns to preserve

- **Feature naming**: kebab-case in `[features]` (`runtime-tokio`), snake-case in `pub use` aliases (`runtime_tokio`). They must stay paired across the facade's `Cargo.toml` and `src/lib.rs`.
- **`paigasus-helikon-cli` uses `autobins = false`** because the `paigasus-helikon` (hyphen) binary maps to `src/bin/paigasus_helikon.rs` (underscore — hyphens are illegal in Rust filenames). Removing `autobins = false` reintroduces a phantom `paigasus_helikon` binary that conflicts with the explicit `[[bin]]` entry.
- **`paigasus-helikon-macros` is a proc-macro crate from day one** (`[lib] proc-macro = true`). Don't convert it to a regular lib even though it currently has no macros.
- **The `paigasus-helikon` facade lib shares its name with the `paigasus-helikon` CLI binary by design** (Notion ref's "fully-qualified shim alias"). This produces a non-fatal `cargo doc` filename-collision warning. Don't "fix" it by renaming either — both names are user-facing API. The accepted future fix is `doc = false` on the CLI binary entry.
- **License is dual `Apache-2.0 OR MIT`** (decided 2026-05-20, reversing the 2026-05-16 MIT-only call). Both `LICENSE-APACHE` and `LICENSE-MIT` live at the repo root; the workspace metadata is `license = "Apache-2.0 OR MIT"`. Per Rust ecosystem convention — no Apache-only or MIT-only crates in the workspace. Contributions are accepted under the same dual license by default (the standard inbound-equals-outbound clause is restated in `README.md`).
- **MSRV is `1.94`** (workspace-package level; raised from 1.85 in SMA-329 because sqlx 0.9.0 declares `rust-version = "1.94.0"` — the pre-existing highest floor in the workspace). If a dep raises MSRV, bump `rust-version` to what cargo demands rather than downgrading the dep.
- **Workspace-wide `missing_docs` enforcement** lives in root `Cargo.toml` (`[workspace.lints.rust] missing_docs = "warn"`). Each non-CLI crate opts in with `[lints] workspace = true`. The CLI overrides locally with `[lints.rust] missing_docs = "allow"` and does **not** include `workspace = true` — cargo treats `[lints] workspace = true` and an inline `[lints.<tool>]` table as mutually exclusive. When adding a new crate, copy the opt-in block. When adding a new `pub use` re-export to the facade, give it a `///` doc comment or `-D warnings` will fail the docs job.
- **`cargo msrv` has no `--workspace` flag.** The msrv workflow verifies one representative inheriting crate: `cargo msrv --path crates/paigasus-helikon-core verify`. Because every member uses `rust-version.workspace = true`, success on one is success on all. Don't "fix" the workflow by adding `--workspace`; that's what the first SMA-305 CI run died on.
- **Nightly is date-pinned** (`NIGHTLY_TOOLCHAIN: nightly-2026-05-01` at the workflow `env:` level in `ci.yml`, threaded into the doc-coverage script as `NIGHTLY_CHANNEL`). The rustdoc JSON coverage format is `-Z unstable-options` and can shift between nightlies; floating `nightly` would be a CI footgun. Bumping is a one-line follow-up chore, not an emergency.
- **Bootstrap commits on release infrastructure must use `chore(...)` or `docs(...)` types**, never `feat`/`fix`. release-plz parses every commit since the last per-crate tag — a `feat(workspace): ...` commit that touches every `Cargo.toml` would attribute a bump to every crate. The SMA-307 bootstrap PR followed this rule; the same rule applies to any future `release-plz.toml` or `release-plz.yml` edits.

## Model routing

The general tiering rules are in the global `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Only the repo-specific rules are here.

- **Use Opus for release work.** This covers release-plz, the stub-ascend recipe, a hand-bumped crate version, and any red required gate. A wrong answer breaks a publish; see `docs/runbooks/release-ascend.md`.
- **Haiku can read CI output.** Change to Opus when the question becomes *why* a required gate is red.

## Workflow conventions

- Branch per Linear issue: `feature/<sma-####>-<kebab-title>`. The branch name is pre-computed in each Linear ticket's `gitBranchName` field.
- Design artifacts per ticket (`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>.md`) land on the feature branch alongside the implementation — not pre-merged to `main`.
- **Keep the public mdBook (`docs/book/`) current — update it in the same PR as any user-facing change.** Before opening a PR, check whether the work changes public API, the quickstart/example flow, the crate roster (incl. a stub crate ascending to published), or a documented concept; if so, bring the affected `docs/book/src/*.md` page(s) into line on the same branch. The book is published from `main` and drifts silently otherwise — it sat as the untouched SMA-311 scaffold (13/17 pages still `> **Stub.**`) through all of Stage 1 before anyone noticed; SMA-423 is the one-time catch-up, and this rule keeps the backlog from rebuilding. A pure-internal change (refactor, CI, deps, release plumbing) needs no book edit — but make that a conscious call, not a silent skip. `mdbook build docs/book` must stay clean (`[output.linkcheck] warning-policy = "error"`).
- **Keep crate `README.md` files current — update the affected crate's README in the same PR as any change to its public surface.** Each of the ten published crates' `README.md` is its crates.io (and docs.rs landing-sidebar) page — no crate sets an explicit `readme`, so Cargo uses the default `README.md`. Before opening a PR, for every crate the work touches check whether the change affects that crate's public API / usage example, its install or feature story, or its published status (a stub ascending to published, a renamed/added feature flag); if so, bring its `crates/<crate>/README.md` into line on the same branch — and also the facade `crates/paigasus-helikon/README.md` and the root `README.md` whenever the crate roster or the feature → module map changes. README install snippets deliberately use drift-free `cargo add` (no hardcoded versions), so a routine version bump alone needs no README edit. Like the mdBook, the READMEs drift silently otherwise — they sat as untouched 3-line SMA-304 stubs (`Stub — see SMA-304`) through all of Stage 1 while ten crates shipped real implementations; SMA-424 is the one-time catch-up, and this rule keeps the backlog from rebuilding. A pure-internal change (refactor, CI, deps, release plumbing) needs no README edit — but make that a conscious call, not a silent skip.
- Commit prefix: `<type>(<scope>): SMA-### <message>` (e.g. `feat(facade): SMA-304 ...`).
- **PR titles must satisfy two independent rules from `pr-title.yml`** (`amannn/action-semantic-pull-request`):
  1. **Full Conventional Commits format.** The action enforces a valid `type(scope):` prefix from the action's configured `types` list — independent of the subject regex. `SMA-317 add anthropic provider` (no prefix) fails; `feat(providers-anthropic): SMA-317 add anthropic provider` passes.
  2. **Subject must start lowercase after the `SMA-###` prefix.** The `subjectPattern: ^([A-Z]{2,4}-\d+ )?[^A-Z].+$` rejects `feat(core): SMA-314 LlmAgent + ...` because `L` is uppercase; lead the subject with a lowercase verb (`add`, `wire`, `pin`, `promote`, `implement`, `fix`).
  Per-commit Conventional Commit titles on the feature branch don't trip either rule — only the PR title (which becomes the squashed `main` commit) is gated.
- Linear auto-closes the linked SMA-* issue when its PR merges; no manual status move needed.
- **Always implement GitHub Actions against the latest stable major**, pinned to a commit SHA (never a moving `@vN` tag), keeping the human-readable version as a trailing `# vX.Y.Z` comment **on the `uses:` line**, so the SHA is auditable. The comment must end with the version: Dependabot updates only a same-line comment that ends with the old version, so a version on its own line above the step goes stale on every bump (SMA-744). This rule applies only to pins of a tagged release. `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` is pinned to an untagged `master` commit, so it has no version comment. Do not add one, because no tag gives a correct version. The `gh-actions` Dependabot group sets no `update-types`, so its configuration permits major bumps in the same grouped PR. Do not depend on that: `actions/checkout` still sat on v6.0.2 until SMA-486 bumped it by hand, so **check for a new major by hand**. `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` is a special case: it ships rolling branches and a periodically re-pointed `v1` tag, so confirm the direction (`ahead_by > 0, behind_by == 0`) before accepting any bump — the naive "bump to latest release" recipe once would have proposed an ~11-month downgrade. Independently and permanently: every site pinning it **must** pair the SHA with an explicit `with: toolchain: …`, because a SHA ref carries no toolchain selector. Recipes and history: `docs/runbooks/github-actions-pinning.md`.
- **After a PR merges to `main`, release-plz opens/updates a `chore: release` PR** (authored by the paigasusbot App) carrying the version bumps + CHANGELOG; in the normal flow **merging that PR is what publishes to crates.io** (the merged feature PR left versions matching the registry, so its own `main` push publishes nothing). The exception is a PR that bumps its own version — the stub-ascend ritual — which publishes on its own merge with no separate release PR. Check the release PR after every merge and watch its CI — its release-PR `cargo update` can pull a fresh advisory that reddens `audit`/`deny` on the bot PR **only** (independent of `main`); fix with a `chore(deps)` pin and release-plz regenerates the PR clean.

## CI

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs nine jobs on every PR (`commits` is PR-only; the other eight also run on push to `main`): `fmt`, `clippy`, `test` (matrix `{ubuntu, macos, windows} × {stable, 1.94}`, `fail-fast: false`), `build-no-default-features`, `docs` (`RUSTDOCFLAGS=-D warnings`), `doc-coverage` (gated at `DOC_COVERAGE_THRESHOLD`, default 80%), `commits` (`convco check`), `sessions-it` (Postgres/Redis, path-filtered), and `markdown-lint`. The `paigasus-helikon-cli` crate is excluded from both the `missing_docs` lint and the coverage aggregator until its public API stabilizes.

`.github/workflows/integration.yml` runs `temporal-it` and `agentcore-image` as **signal-only** jobs, deliberately outside `ci.yml` so an expected flake cannot make "ci is red on `main`" meaningless. **Signal-only means *not listed as required*, never `continue-on-error`.**

`.github/workflows/msrv.yml` runs `cargo msrv --path crates/paigasus-helikon-core verify` as a non-required signal that the declared MSRV is truthful.

Supply-chain workflows (`audit.yml`, `deny.yml`, `sbom.yml`) are separate from `ci.yml` because they have independent triggers and failure semantics. `audit.yml` and `deny.yml` both run on push to `main`, PRs, a daily cron, and `workflow_dispatch`, so `main` is re-evaluated daily at exactly PR severity.

**To read an audit verdict, use the Checks API, not the legacy commit-status API** — the latter returns only `CodeRabbit` on this repo, rendering a confident `state: success` that contains no audit verdict whatsoever:

```bash
gh api repos/SMK1085/paigasus-helikon/commits/main/check-runs \
  --jq '.check_runs[] | select(.name=="audit" or .name=="deny") | {name, status, conclusion}'
```

Note also that the `scheduled-audit` job's green status means nothing at any severity — read the *run* conclusion, never that job's status.

The required-status-check contexts gated on `main` are (bare job names, as posted by the GitHub Actions app): `fmt`, `clippy`, `test (ubuntu-latest, stable)`, `test (macos-latest, stable)`, `test (windows-latest, stable)`, `docs`, `doc-coverage`, `book-build`, `commits`, `pr-title`, `audit`, `deny`, `sessions-it`, `build-no-default-features`, `markdown-lint`. The macOS job is required because it is the only gate that compiles and runs the Seatbelt backend; the Windows job because it is the only gate that exercises the Windows timeout path in `paigasus-helikon-tools` — `cmd /C` process spawning and a `TerminateProcess`-based kill, which unlike the unix path has no process-group semantics and assigns a real exit code (SMA-569); `sessions-it` because it is the only gate that runs the live Postgres/Redis session backends; `build-no-default-features` because it is the only gate that compiles `runtime-axum` and `runtime-actix` with default features off. The canonical declaration is `.github/rulesets/main-protection-checks.json` (see CONTRIBUTING.md → "Repo configuration"). Other matrix variants (the `1.94` legs) run as signals only.

These pins are hand-bumped with nothing tracking them: `TEMPORAL_CLI_VERSION`/`TEMPORAL_CLI_SHA256` in `integration.yml`, `NIGHTLY_TOOLCHAIN` in `ci.yml`, `convco@…` in `ci.yml`'s `commits` job, `MDBOOK_VERSION`/`MDBOOK_LINKCHECK_VERSION` in `docs.yml`, and `markdownlint-cli2` via `package-lock.json`. **A checksum mismatch is never a signal to update the digest** — the causes are, in order, a truncated download, an upstream re-tag, and tampering; verify upstream independently first.

**The workspace needs no system `protoc`** (SMA-623): `temporalio-client`'s `vendored-protox` feature compiles the Temporal protos with `protox`. `ci.yml` sets `PROTOC` to a path that does not exist, and `build-no-default-features` asserts that the feature is active. If a build fails with "Could not find `protoc`", do not add a `protoc` install — find which build script calls it. Rationale and recovery: `docs/runbooks/ci-architecture.md` → "protoc and protox".

Job-by-job rationale, the audit/deny signal semantics, and the incident history behind all of the above: `docs/runbooks/ci-architecture.md`.

**GitHub's 10 GB Actions cache limit is a standing constraint, not a one-time cleanup** (SMA-618): it is GitHub's **default**, not a hard ceiling — a repo admin, org owner or enterprise owner can raise it (user-owned repos up to 10 TB) at additional storage cost, and SMA-618 deliberately chose to fit inside it rather than pay. Enforced at 10 **GiB** (10,737,418,240 bytes) despite the "10 GB" wording. Going over fails nothing — it just triggers silent LRU eviction that makes CI legs run cold at random. `cache-budget.yml` monitors it daily and warns (never fails) above 8.5 GiB. - **`pre-push`** — runs `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and `convco check <merge-base>..HEAD`. Catches the three fastest CI gates pre-push; deliberately omits `cargo test` and `cargo doc` (too slow for every push). Bypass for WIP branches: `git push --no-verify`.

Three rules here are easy to get wrong, and each has already cost a debugging session:

- **The re-install silently does nothing inside a git worktree** — cargo-husky searches for a `.git` *directory* and a worktree's is a file, so it installs nothing and the old hook keeps running. Run the re-install from the **main checkout**, and verify with `grep` against the installed copy rather than assuming.
- **Never hand-copy a hook onto `.git/hooks/<name>`** — on this machine the Entire CLI owns `pre-push` and chains to `.git/hooks/pre-push.pre-entire`, which is where the cargo-husky hook actually lives. Check for a `.pre-entire` sibling first and install into that slot.
- **The convco baseline must be a merge-base, not a branch tip** — `convco check A..B` silently falls back to walking the entire history when `A` is not an ancestor of `B`, rejecting correct branches with failures the author did not write.

Mechanics and the SMA-547 postmortem: `docs/runbooks/local-hooks.md`.

## Fixture line endings

`.gitattributes` pins `crates/paigasus-helikon-providers-anthropic/tests/fixtures/*.txt` to `text eol=lf`. The streaming tests `include_str!` the SSE fixtures and split them on literal `\n` delimiters; without this, Windows checkouts produce CRLF bytes and the literal-string splits return one part instead of two. When adding wire-format fixtures elsewhere that the test code parses byte-level, extend the rule.
